figures.caption: Every distance at once. The darkest entries (orange) are the diameter, 4. The right-hand column is each person's eccentricity: their distance to whoever is farthest. The mean of the 90 off-diagonal entries is 1.978.
figures.alt: A ten by ten table of distances between the ten friends. The diagonal is zero, and every entry is between 1 and 4. The entries equal to 4 are shaded orange and sit in the rows and columns of Jo and of Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli. A right-hand column lists each person's largest distance.

figures.caption: Repeated search. One breadth-first search from each person gives one row of the table. Five people, five searches, five rows.
figures.alt: Five small copies of the five-person network. In each, a different person is the starting point and every dot shows its distance from that person. Below, a five by five table whose rows are colored to match the five searches that produced them.

figures.caption: The one move that Floyd-Warshall repeats. For a pair of people and one allowed stopover, keep whichever is shorter: the best known ride, or the two rides joined at the stopover.
figures.alt: Three dots in a triangle: Ana at the left, Ben at the right and Cleo above between them. A gray line from Ana to Ben is labeled 9 minutes. Two orange lines, Ana to Cleo at 2 minutes and Cleo to Ben at 3 minutes, are the detour. The text says 2 plus 3 is 5, which beats 9.

figures.caption: Floyd-Warshall on five places and travel minutes. Each step allows one more person as a stopover and rewrites any cell that the new stopover improves (orange). The blue row and column belong to the stopover being added. After the fifth step the table is final.
figures.alt: Six five by five tables of travel minutes. The first holds only the direct rides, with infinity where there is no direct ride. Each next table allows one more stopover, in the order Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev, Eli, and highlights cells that got smaller. The last table has no infinity left and every entry is a shortest travel time.

figures.caption: Johnson's reweighting. Each person gets a score (the cheapest way to reach them from a helper tied to everyone at cost 0). Adding the starting score and subtracting the ending score to each cost removes the negative cost, and every route between the same two people shifts by the same amount.
figures.alt: Two copies of a four-person directed network. On the left the tie from Ben to Cleo costs minus 2 and is drawn in red. On the right every cost has been adjusted using scores of 0, 0, minus 2 and 0 for Ana, Ben, Cleo and Dev, so all costs are zero or more.

figures.caption: Rough counts of basic steps (not seconds) to fill the whole table. Floyd-Warshall pays for every triple of people no matter how few ties there are. Repeated search and Johnson pay in proportion to the ties.
figures.alt: Four groups of three horizontal bars on a log scale, one group per network size. In every group the Floyd-Warshall bar is longest. For the sparse networks the other two bars are two to three powers of ten shorter. For the 1,000 person network with 100,000 ties the three bars are closer together.

figures.caption: Memory for a full distance table at 4 bytes per entry. Ten times more people means a hundred times more table, which is why very large networks answer distance questions without ever writing the whole table down.
figures.alt: Four horizontal bars on a log scale. Each is a hundred times longer than the one above: 4 megabytes for a thousand people, 400 megabytes for ten thousand, 40 gigabytes for a hundred thousand and 4 terabytes for a million. The last two are drawn in red.

figures.caption: Eccentricity is a person's distance to whoever is farthest from them. The people with the smallest value (radius 2) form the center; those with the largest (diameter 4) sit on the edge.
figures.alt: On the left, the ten-person network. Hana, with eccentricity 2, is the one green square. Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev, Eli and Jo, with eccentricity 4, are orange circles; Fay, Gus and Ivo, at 3, are blue circles. On the right, ten horizontal bars sorted by eccentricity.

figures.caption: A network in two pieces. Averaging only the pairs that can reach each other gives a small, friendly number and hides that 18 of the 30 ordered pairs cannot reach each other at all. Report how many pairs are cut off, or use a measure that counts them.
figures.alt: Two groups of three people each, tied within the group and not between groups. Beside them, a six by six table of distances: the two three by three blocks along the diagonal hold 0, 1 and 2, and the rest is infinity, shaded orange. Below, two averages: 1.17 over reachable pairs, and 0.37 when unreachable pairs count as zero efficiency.

figures.caption: Same five people, two rules. In a queue the first to arrive is served first; in a stack the last to arrive is served first.
figures.alt: Left, five numbered people in a line labeled queue, with an arrow marking Ana at the front as OUT and an arrow at the back marking Eli as IN. Right, five plates stacked with Eli on top, labeled stack, with a single arrow at the top for both IN and OUT.

figures.caption: A heap of seven tasks. The picture is a tree, the storage is a plain list, and the family tree is slot arithmetic. The smallest number is always in slot 0.
figures.alt: Left, a tree of seven circles: 2 at the top, then 5 and 3, then 9, 6, 4 and 8, with names Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev, Eli, Fay and Gus underneath. Right, the same seven numbers as a row of seven boxes numbered 0 to 6, and the slot rules: children of slot i are slots 2i plus 1 and 2i plus 2; the parent is slot (i minus 1) over 2 rounded down.

figures.caption: Inserting 1 into the heap. It starts in the last slot and floats up, swapping with each bigger parent, until it reaches the top. Only the nodes on one path from bottom to top are touched.
figures.alt: Four small heaps in a two by two grid, each a tree above a row of boxes. Step 1 places a 1 at the bottom, under 9. Step 2 swaps it with 9. Step 3 swaps it with 5. Step 4 swaps it with 2, leaving 1 at the top. Each panel has a one-line note.

figures.caption: Removing the smallest. The last task jumps into the empty top slot and sinks, each time swapping with the smaller of its two children, until the rule holds again.
figures.alt: Four small heaps of seven tasks in a two by two grid. Step 1 shows the last task moved into the top. Steps 2 and 3 show it swapping downward with the smaller child. Step 4 shows the finished heap with the new smallest number on top.

figures.caption: Union-find on five people. Joining two groups means hanging one root under the other, a single change. When we later ask who Eli's group leader is, we point Eli straight at the leader so the next question is faster.
figures.alt: Four panels, each a small forest of circles holding the initials A, B, C, D and E, with a row of five boxes of parent numbers below. Panel 1: five separate roots. Panel 2: Ben hangs under Ana and Eli under Dev. Panel 3: Dev's tree is hung under Ana, so Ana is the root of Ana, Ben, Dev and Eli, with Cleo alone. Panel 4: Eli points directly at Ana.

figures.caption: A hash map sends each key through a scrambling rule to a bucket, then looks only in that bucket. Two keys can land in the same bucket (orange), which is why we still check names inside it.
figures.alt: Seven names on the left, each with its alphabet-place sum and remainder after dividing by 7, joined by lines to seven buckets in the middle. Ben and Cleo share bucket 0 and Eli and Gus share bucket 5, drawn in orange. Notes on the right explain the lookup and collisions.

figures.caption: A bitset holds a group of people as one row of switches. AND finds who is in both groups, OR finds who is in either, and a count of the ones tells the group's size.
figures.alt: Four rows of eight boxes, each 0 or 1, for people 0 to 7. Ana's friends have ones at 0, 2, 3 and 6; Dev's friends at 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7. The AND row has ones at 2, 3 and 6, three people; the OR row has ones at 0, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7, six people.

figures.caption: Radix sort on seven numbers. Each pass looks at one digit (orange) and files the numbers into ten buckets, then reads them back out. After three passes, the list is in order.
figures.alt: Four columns of the same seven three-digit numbers: the start (329, 457, 657, 839, 436, 720, 355), then after sorting by the ones digit, the tens digit and the hundreds digit. The digit used in each pass is orange. The last column reads 329, 355, 436, 457, 657, 720, 839.

passes: After sorting by the ones digit
After sorting by the tens digit
After sorting by the hundreds digit

figures.caption: The building blocks side by side. Most do their basic job in one step or a handful; the heap and sorts pay a logarithm for keeping order.
figures.alt: A table with eight rows and four columns: block, cost to add, cost to take or find, and what it is good for. Queue, stack, union-find, hash map and bitset are one step or close to it. The heap costs log n steps to add and to take. A comparing sort costs n log n and radix sort k passes over n.

figures.caption: A connected component is an island: everyone on it can reach everyone else on it, and nobody can reach anyone off it. This network of eleven people has four islands. Kai, with no ties, is an island of one.
figures.alt: Eleven people drawn in four dashed boxes. The largest box holds Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli, tied together. Next, Fay, Gus and Hana in a chain. Then Ivo and Jo, tied to each other. Kai sits alone in the fourth box. There are no ties between boxes.

figures.caption: Finding components by search. Pick someone with no label, search outward from them and give everyone you reach the next label. Repeat until nobody is unlabeled. Four searches, four islands.
figures.alt: Four copies of the eleven-person network. In the first, only the five-person island is labeled 1. In the second, the three-person island is added, labeled 2. In the third, the two-person island is labeled 3. In the fourth, Kai is labeled 4 and every person has a label.

figures.caption: Union-find on eight people. Each person points to someone in their group, and the group's leader points to nobody. Joining two groups makes the smaller group's leader point to the bigger group's leader. Each tie is one tiny edit.
figures.alt: Six snapshots of eight people. At the start there are eight separate groups. After one tie, Ana and Ben form a group. After three ties there is a group of four and two singletons. After four, five, and seven ties the groups merge until, after tie seven, all eight people hang under one leader in a short tree.

figures.caption: Path compression. A lookup walks up to the group's leader; on the way back it makes every person it passed point straight at the leader. The next lookup from any of them is one hop.
figures.alt: Left: six people stacked in a chain, each pointing at the one above, Ana at the top, so Fay is five hops below. Right: Ana at the top with the other five people in a row below her, each pointing directly at Ana with an orange arrow.

figures.caption: Union-find reads ties one at a time and always knows the current groups. Here the ten friends start as ten separate groups and are one group after tie 18, though eighteen ties arrive in all.
figures.alt: A line chart over eighteen ties. The solid blue line, number of groups, falls from 10 and reaches 1 after tie 18. The dashed orange line, size of the biggest group, rises from 1 to 10 over the same ties.

figures.caption: Below about one tie per person the biggest island holds a tiny share of the people. Just past one tie per person, a giant island swallows most of the network. The dots are simulations, found with union-find; the line is the standard large-network formula.
figures.alt: A curve rising from near zero at an average of one tie per person to about 80 percent at two and 98 percent at four. Orange dots from simulated networks of a thousand people sit on a blue formula curve. A dashed vertical line marks one tie per person.

figures.caption: One-way ties. Ignoring direction, these nine people form one weakly connected piece. Following the arrows, they split into 4 strongly connected blocks, where everyone in a block can reach everyone else in it.
figures.alt: Two copies of a nine-person network with arrows. On the left they form one connected picture. On the right they are grouped into four boxes: Ana, Ben and Cleo; Dev, Eli and Fay; Gus and Hana; and Ivo alone. Arrows between boxes only point one way, from left to right.

figures.caption: Tarjan's method on the nine-person network. Each person gets a visit number and a low number (the lowest visit number they can get back to). A person whose low equals their visit number is the leader of a block, and the block is everyone above them on the stack.
figures.alt: The nine-person directed network with each dot labeled with two numbers. Below, a table of the first steps of the search with the stack contents, and a list of the 4 blocks in the order the method finds them: Gus, Hana; Ivo; Dev, Eli, Fay; Ana, Ben, Cleo.

figures.caption: Kosaraju's method. Pass 1 searches the network and notes the order in which each person finishes. Pass 2 reverses every arrow and starts searches in the opposite of that order. Each search in pass 2 collects exactly one strongly connected block.
figures.alt: Two copies of the nine-person network. On the left, each person is labeled with the order in which their search finished. On the right, every arrow is reversed, each person is labeled with their place in the reverse order, and they are colored by block: Ana, Ben, Cleo; Dev, Eli, Fay; Gus, Hana; Ivo.

figures.caption: Condensation. Replace each strongly connected block by a single dot and keep the arrows between blocks. What is left never loops back on itself, so it can be read as a map that flows one way.
figures.alt: On the left, the nine-person network with four boxes around the blocks. On the right, four dots sized by block, with arrows between them: the block of Ana, Ben and Cleo leads to the block of Dev, Eli and Fay, which leads both to Ivo and to the block of Gus and Hana, and Ivo leads to Gus and Hana. There are no arrows back.

figures.caption: Counting by hand. To be sure Ana and Dev are not tied, the edge list makes us read all five rows. The adjacency list takes us to Ana's own list, and her list has one entry.
figures.alt: Left, the five-row edge list with each row numbered 1 to 5 in order, labeled as five rows looked at. Right, a single arrow from Ana to her list holding just Ben's id, labeled as two steps: jump to Ana's list and look at its one entry.

figures.caption: Four growth rates drawn on one chart. For a small number of people they all look harmless; by 20 people the red line is above a million steps and the chart cannot hold it.
figures.alt: A line chart of steps against the number of people from 0 to 20. A green straight line reaches 20. A blue line that bends slightly upward reaches about 86. An orange curve reaches 400 at 20 people. A red curve shoots off the top of the chart at about 9 people. A legend lists the four rates and the step counts at 20 people: 20, 86, 400 and 1,048,576.

figures.caption: What doubling does. A single pass takes twice as long, a sort a little more than twice, every pair four times, every triple eight times. Trying every subset does not just multiply the work, it squares it.
figures.alt: Five horizontal bars. One pass over everything is a bar for 2 times. Sorting is slightly longer, about 2.2 times. Every pair is 4 times and every triple 8 times. The last bar, try every subset, runs off the end of the chart with the note that 2 to the 1,000 becomes 2 to the 2,000.

figures.caption: Wall-clock time for a computer doing a billion simple steps a second. A single pass is fine at any size; every pair is fine at a thousand people and hopeless at a billion.
figures.alt: A grid of four growth rates by three network sizes (1,000; 1,000,000; 1,000,000,000 people). One pass takes a microsecond, a millisecond and one second. Sorting takes 10 microseconds, 20 milliseconds and 30 seconds. Every pair takes one millisecond, 17 minutes and about 32 years. Every triple takes one second, about 32 years and longer than the universe has existed.

figures.caption: The memory story. If one nanosecond lasted a second, your desk (the cache) would answer in a second, the shelf (main memory) in about a minute and a half, and the archive (a drive) in more than a day.
figures.alt: Three boxes side by side. Left, a desk with a few notes, labeled the processor's cache, about 1 second. Middle, a shelf of binders across the room, labeled main memory, about a minute and a half. Right, a building of filing cabinets across town, labeled a solid-state drive, more than a day.

figures.caption: A cache line is an armful of neighbors fetched together. Reading five numbers that sit side by side costs about two armfuls; reading five scattered numbers costs five.
figures.alt: Two grids of 40 numbered slots, five rows of eight, each row framed as one cache line. On the left, slots 6 to 10 are highlighted and sit in two rows, so two lines are fetched. On the right, slots 1, 12, 19, 27 and 36 are highlighted, one in each row, so five lines are fetched.

figures.caption: Speedup from extra workers when only part of the job can be shared. If half is shareable you never beat 2 times, however many workers you hire; at 99 percent, 64 workers give about 39 times.
figures.alt: A line chart of speedup against number of workers from 1 to 64 on a log axis. A dashed diagonal shows perfect speedup. Three curves bend away below it: 50 percent shareable flattens at about 2 times, 90 percent reaches about 8.8 times at 64 workers, and 99 percent reaches about 39 times.

figures.caption: Floating-point addition is not associative. Ten quadrillion plus 1 rounds back to ten quadrillion, so the order of the additions decides whether the 1s survive.
figures.alt: Three rows, each adding the same four numbers (1e16, 1, minus 1e16 and 1) in a different order. As listed gives 1, letting the big ones cancel first gives 2, and adding the big one and both 1s before the other big one gives 0. A note says the true sum is 2.

figures.caption: Each worker adds up its own share; the total depends on the order in which the shares are combined. If that order changes from run to run, so do the last digits.
figures.alt: Two rows of eight numbered workers joined by arrows in two different orders, the same eight numbers in each. Run 1 ends at 377675.59268641757 and run 2 at 377675.59268641751; underneath, the exact sum is 377675.59268641757.

figures.caption: Counting shortest routes. One breadth-first search from the top left also counts: each person's number is the sum of the numbers of the neighbors one step closer. The far corner has 10 shortest routes.
figures.alt: A grid of twelve people in three rows and four columns. The top-left dot is 1. The first row reads 1, 1, 1, 1, the second 1, 2, 3, 4 and the third 1, 3, 6, 10. Darker shading marks people farther from the start. The bottom-right dot shows 10.

figures.caption: Number of shortest routes from Jo to each person. Orange ties are the ones on some shortest route. Only Dev has two shortest routes from Jo (one through Fay, one through Gus); everyone else has exactly one.
figures.alt: The ten-person network with each dot showing a count from Jo. Jo shows 1, Ivo 1, Hana 1, Fay 1, Gus 1, then Ana 1, Ben 1, Cleo 1, Dev 2 and Eli 1. Ties that lie on a shortest route from Jo are orange and thick; the others are thin and gray.

figures.caption: Backtracking. From Ana the search tries each neighbor, then that person's neighbors, never stepping on someone already on the route. Green leaves are routes to Eli (4 of them); gray leaves are dead ends where the search backs up.
figures.alt: On the left, a network of Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli. On the right, a tree that starts at Ana and branches into every route the search tries. Four branches end at Eli and are drawn green. Other branches end at someone who has no unvisited neighbor and are drawn gray.

figures.caption: The first four routes from Ana to Gus, shortest first. Three tie at 2 steps (through Ben, Dev or Fay); the fourth takes 3. 48 routes exist in all that never repeat a person.
figures.alt: Four copies of the ten-person network. In each, one route from Ana to Gus is drawn thickly. The first three routes have 2 steps and go through Ben, through Dev and through Fay. The fourth route has 3 steps.

figures.caption: Counting walks is easy (multiply the tie table by itself) and the answer keeps growing. Counting routes that never repeat a person is a different question, and for Ana to Eli it stays at 4.
figures.alt: A bar chart on a log scale of the number of walks from Ana to Eli of each length from 1 to 10. There are none for lengths 1 and 2, then 2, 2, and so on, growing steadily to 1160. A dashed blue line at 4 marks the routes that never repeat anyone.

figures.caption: Routes between opposite corners of a 4 by 4 grid, by length. There are 20 shortest routes (6 steps) and 184 in all. Most routes are long and winding.
figures.alt: A bar chart with one bar for each route length from 6 to 14 steps. The first bar, in blue, is 20. The bars grow to a peak and shrink again. The bars add up to 184.

figures.caption: Routes between opposite corners of a square grid of people. Shortest routes grow steadily (252 on a 6 by 6 grid). Routes that never repeat a person grow wildly: 1,262,816 on a 6 by 6 grid, and each extra person per side multiplies the count by more than the last.
figures.alt: A line chart on a log scale. The blue line for shortest routes climbs from 2 on a 2 by 2 grid to 924 on a 7 by 7 grid. The red dashed line for all routes that never repeat a person climbs much faster: 2, 12, 184, 8,512, then 1,262,816 for the 6 by 6 grid, where it stops. A table at the right lists the same numbers.

figures.caption: Capping the work honestly. A listing that stops at a limit must say it stopped and report its result as a lower bound. On this 6 by 6 grid the true count is 1,262,816, over a hundred times the limit.
figures.alt: Two cards. The left one, green, reports a limit of 10,000 routes, 10,000 listed, stopped by the limit, so at least 10,000. The right one, red and dashed, reports 10,000 routes found and says nothing about the limit, leaving the reader to think that is the total, when the true total is 1,262,816.

figures.caption: Five people, numbered from zero. The numbers are what the computer stores; the names are for us.
figures.alt: A five-person network. Ana (0) is tied to Ben (1). Ben is tied to Cleo (2) and Dev (3), who are tied to each other, and Dev is tied to Eli (4). To the right, the five ids 0 to 4 sit above the names Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli.

figures.caption: Ids versus labels. The file may use badge numbers or usernames; the engine wants 0 to n minus 1, so a lookup table translates once on the way in and back on the way out.
figures.alt: Three columns. On the left, five badge numbers from a file: 4017 for Ana, 52 for Ben, 9 for Cleo, 3180 for Dev and 77 for Eli. In the middle, a lookup table pairing each badge number with a position 0 to 4. On the right, the five positions as numbered dots. Arrows run left to right.

figures.caption: The edge list: the network as a plain list of pairs. It is the format files arrive in, and the easiest to add to.
figures.alt: The five-person network on the left with the Ben-Dev tie highlighted. On the right, a two-column table of five rows: 0 and 1, 1 and 2, 1 and 3, 2 and 3, 3 and 4. The row 1 and 3 is highlighted and labeled Ben-Dev.

figures.caption: The adjacency list: every person points to a short list of their neighbors. Asking who Ben knows is now one step to Ben's list.
figures.alt: Five rows, one per person, each with a numbered dot and a name. An arrow leads from each person to a chain of boxes holding the neighbor ids: Ana 1; Ben 0, 2, 3; Cleo 1, 3; Dev 1, 2, 4; Eli 3. Each chain ends with the word end. A note on the right says each list lives in its own spot in memory.

figures.caption: CSR keeps the whole network in two flat lists. The first says where each person's friends start; the second holds everyone's friends one after another.
figures.alt: Two rows of numbered boxes. The top row, offsets, holds 0, 1, 4, 6, 9, 10, one box for each person plus a last one. The bottom row, targets, holds 1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, shaded in five colors, one color for each person's block of friends. A bracket over slots 6, 7 and 8 is labeled Dev's friends and arrows lead to it from offsets 6 and 9.

figures.caption: The adjacency matrix: one cell for every possible pair, with a 1 where a tie exists. Checking one pair is instant; the price is that nearly all the cells are empty in a big network.
figures.alt: A five by five grid with the people's names along the top and left. Ones mark the ties; the grid is a mirror image across the diagonal. Ben's row, shaded orange, has ones under Ana, Cleo and Dev. A note counts 25 cells and 10 ones.

figures.caption: Bit rows pack each row of the matrix into a few machine words. One AND of two rows answers a question about 64 people at once; here it finds that Ben and Dev both know Cleo.
figures.alt: A five by five grid of zeros and ones, one row per person, with each row also shown as a single number: 2, 13, 10, 22 and 8. Underneath, the rows for Ben and Dev are placed side by side with the word AND between them and a result row that has a single one, in column 2, which is Cleo.

figures.caption: Directed and weighted: arrows mean each person lists only the people they point to, and weights ride along in a third array that lines up slot for slot with the targets.
figures.alt: On the left, the five-person network with arrows and a number on each: Ana to Ben 3, Ben to Cleo 5, Ben to Dev 2, Dev to Cleo 4, Dev and Eli pointing at each other with 1 and 6. On the right, three rows of boxes: offsets 0, 1, 3, 3, 5, 6; targets 1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 3; weights 3, 5, 2, 4, 1, 6. Notes explain that each weight lines up with the target in the same slot.

figures.caption: Memory against network size on a log scale (each gridline is a thousand times more). The three list layouts grow in step with the people; the matrix grows with the square of them and passes a laptop's memory around 100,000 people.
figures.alt: A chart on logarithmic axes, number of people from 100 to 1,000,000 across and memory from 1 kilobyte to 10 terabytes up. Three nearly parallel straight lines for the edge list, adjacency list and CSR end near 40 to 64 megabytes at a million people. Two steeper lines for the matrix and bit rows end at 1 terabyte and 125 gigabytes, crossing a dashed line at 16 gigabytes, a laptop's memory, before a million people.

figures.caption: No layout wins everywhere. Lists are quick at who knows whom; the matrix is quick at whether two people are tied; bit rows are quick at comparing two people.
figures.alt: A grid with five rows for the layouts and five columns for questions. Each cell reads fast, so-so or slow with a tick, tilde or cross. The edge list is fast only at visiting every tie. Adjacency list and CSR are fast at listing and counting a person's friends and visiting every tie. The matrix is fast at checking one pair only. Bit rows are fast at checking a pair, counting friends and finding common friends.

figures.caption: Two routes from Ana to Eli. The dashed orange route has the fewest steps (2) but takes 12 minutes. The solid blue route has more steps (3) and takes only 9. When ties cost different amounts, counting steps is the wrong question.
figures.alt: The ten-person network with the minutes written on each tie. A dashed orange route runs Ana, Ben, Eli and is labeled 2 steps, 12 minutes. A solid blue route runs Ana, Cleo, Dev, Eli and is labeled 3 steps, 9 minutes.

figures.caption: Dijkstra's algorithm on the travel-time network, one person at a time. Each turn settles the waiting person with the smallest guess, then lets that person improve their neighbours' guesses. Look at Dev: first guessed at 9 from Ana directly, then improved to 7 once Cleo was settled.
figures.alt: A table of ten turns. Turn 1 settles Ana at 0 and sets guesses for Ben 6, Cleo 2, Dev 9 and Fay 8. Turn 2 settles Cleo at 2 and improves Dev from 9 to 7. Turn 3 settles Ben at 6. Turn 4 settles Dev at 7 and improves Eli to 9. Later turns settle Fay at 8, Eli at 9, Gus at 12, Hana at 13, Ivo at 17 and Jo at 20.

rows: Ben ? to 6, Cleo ? to 2, Dev ? to 9, Fay ? to 8

figures.caption: The reason Dijkstra's algorithm is correct. The waiting person with the smallest guess cannot be beaten by any other route, because any other route leaves the settled region through a waiting person whose guess is at least as large, and costs are never negative.
figures.alt: Three nested circles. The innermost, in blue, holds settled people around a start marked 0. A middle ring in orange holds the waiting people. The outer dashed circle holds people not yet met. A legend on the right explains the three groups.

figures.caption: One negative tie is enough to break the rule 'a settled person's distance is final'. The rule settles a at 2, but the route s, b, a costs 5 + (-4) = 1. Bellman-Ford, which never treats a distance as final, gets it right.
figures.alt: A directed network of five people s, a, b, c, d. Ties: s to a costs 2, s to b costs 5, b to a costs -4 (drawn in red), a to c costs 3, b to c costs 6 and c to d costs 1. Below it, the settling rule gives distances [0, 2, 5, 5, 6] and the correct answer is [0, 1, 5, 4, 5].

figures.caption: Bellman-Ford tries every tie once per round. On the left network it stops improving after a few rounds. On the right, a loop whose ties add up to less than zero keeps shaving the distances forever, which is how the algorithm notices the trap.
figures.alt: Two tables of distances for five people s, a, b, c, d, one row per round. The left table fills in over three rounds and then stops changing. In the right table, the numbers for a, b and c keep decreasing in every round shown, with the later rows shaded.

figures.caption: Dijkstra and A* on a grid of streets with a wall. Both return a route of 14 steps. Dijkstra settled 88 places, A* only 41, because it ranks places by distance so far plus a guess of the distance still to go.
figures.alt: Two grids of thirteen columns by seven rows with a short vertical black wall in the middle, covering the third to fifth rows. A start S sits in the middle row near the left edge and a target T in the middle row near the right edge. On the left, 88 squares are shaded, almost the whole grid. On the right, 41 squares are shaded, a narrower band between S and T. An orange route runs from S, bends around the end of the wall and reaches T, in both.

figures.caption: In a network where the number of people reached keeps multiplying, two small searches that meet in the middle touch far fewer people than one big search that goes the whole way. The pairs are sorted by the one-sided cost.
figures.alt: A bar chart on a log scale with ten pairs of bars. Each pair has a red bar for a one-sided search and a blue bar, much shorter, for a two-sided search. The one-sided bars run from about 5,132 to 19,837 people; the two-sided bars run from about 91 to 658.

figures.caption: A decision table for shortest paths. The first two columns are the questions to ask of your network; the last is the reason to pick anything fancier than Dijkstra.
figures.alt: A table with five rows: breadth-first, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, A star and bidirectional. Columns give what the ties may cost, whether negative costs are allowed (only Bellman-Ford), what each answers (distances from one start, or one route from start to goal), and when it wins.

rows: negative costs, or checking for traps
you can guess distance to go
you know both ends, network is big

figures.caption: The only difference between the two searches is how the waiting list is kept. A queue serves whoever has waited longest. A stack serves whoever arrived last.
figures.alt: Left: five circles in a row labeled Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli, with Ana at the front, an arrow showing service at the front and another showing new people joining at the back. Right: four plates labeled Ana, Ben, Cleo and Dev stacked with Dev on top, with an arrow putting a new plate on top and another taking one off the top.

figures.caption: The same network, rearranged so that everyone sits in the column of their distance from Ana. Every tie goes from a column to the same one or the next one, never further, which is why the search can be trusted to find shortest routes.
figures.alt: Five columns headed Ana, 1 step, 2 steps, 3 steps and 4 steps. Ana is alone in the first. Ben, Cleo, Dev and Fay are in the second; Eli, Gus and Hana in the third; Ivo in the fourth; Jo in the fifth. Thick blue lines mark the tie that found each person and dashed grey lines mark the other ties.

figures.caption: A depth-first search from Ana. The numbers are the order people were first met. It runs Ana, Ben, Dev, Cleo, Fay, Gus, Eli, then backs up and finishes with Hana, Ivo and Jo: it goes as deep as it can before it ever tries another friend.
figures.alt: The ten-person network. Each person has a number from 1 to 10. Ana is 1, Ben 2, Dev 3, Cleo 4, Fay 5, Gus 6, Eli 7, Hana 8, Ivo 9 and Jo 10. Nine ties are drawn thick orange and the other nine are thin dashed grey. A list on the right narrates the first steps, including the places the search hits a dead end and backs up.

figures.caption: Same streets, same starting corner, same answer to 'who can I reach?', and very different orders. Breadth-first finds everything near the start first, in rings. Depth-first picks one direction and goes until it hits a wall.
figures.alt: Two grids of nine columns by seven rows, each square numbered from 1 to 63 by the order of discovery and shaded from light to dark. On the left the numbers grow outward from the circled middle square in diamond-shaped rings. On the right the numbers follow one long winding path that sweeps up and across the grid before coming back for the squares it skipped.

figures.caption: One breadth-first search from Ana leaves three things behind for free: every person's distance, the person who found them, and therefore a shortest route to anyone, read backwards. The orange row is Jo.
figures.alt: A table with columns Person, Steps from Ana, Found by and Route from Ana, with ten rows in the order people were found. Ana has 0 steps. Ben, Cleo, Dev and Fay have 1 step, all found by Ana. Eli, Gus and Hana have 2 steps, found by Ben, Ben and Fay. Ivo has 3 steps found by Hana. Jo has 4 steps, found by Ivo, with route Ana to Fay to Hana to Ivo to Jo.

figures.caption: Counting islands. Search from the first person who has not been found yet, then again from the next one still unfound, and so on. The number of searches you needed is the number of islands.
figures.alt: Twelve circles in four groups. Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli form a blue group numbered 1. Fay, Gus, Hana and Ivo form an orange group numbered 2. Jo and Kai form a green group numbered 3. Lena sits alone in a purple group numbered 4.

figures.caption: Double the network and a search does about double the work (the blue line is nearly straight on this log scale with a slope of one). Checking every pair of people grows much faster (the dashed red line).
figures.alt: A chart with the number of people from 250 to 32,000 along the bottom on a log scale and steps of work up the side on a log scale. A solid blue line with circles rises gently from about 1,000 to about 128,000. A dashed red line rises much more steeply from about 31,000 to about 512 million.

figures.caption: Why this chapter comes early: most later algorithms are one of these two walks with a little extra bookkeeping.
figures.alt: Six rounded cards in two rows of three. Blue cards for breadth-first: How far (distances and shortest routes) and What is nearby (everyone within two steps). A green card for either: Who is connected (islands). Orange cards for depth-first: Is there a loop, What comes first (ordering tasks), and Where does it split (bridges and cut people).

figures.caption: One question (how close is each person to everyone else?) on a network with two islands, answered four ways. Two honest tools can print different numbers, and even rank Ben and Eli in a different order, without either having a bug.
figures.alt: On the left, a path of four people (Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev) and a separate pair (Eli, Fay). On the right, a bar chart with four groups of two bars, for Ben and Eli. First group, Ben 0.75 and Eli 1.00. Second group, Ben 0.45 and Eli 0.20. Third group, both 0.00. Fourth group, Ben 0.50 and Eli 0.20.

figures.caption: The basic move of testing: give two independent sources the same question, compare the answers, and treat any difference as something to explain.
figures.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows. A blue box, Same input, sends arrows to an orange box, Your routine, and a purple box, Reference. Both of those send arrows to a green box, Compare, which leads to two outcomes: agree, carry on; differ, find out why.

figures.caption: A tiny case with answers worked out by hand. If a routine cannot get these right, nothing larger is worth running.
figures.alt: A five-person network: Ana is tied to Ben and to Cleo; Ben and Cleo are each tied to Dev; Dev is tied to Eli. A table lists each person's number of ties (2, 2, 2, 3, 1), the steps from Ana (0, 1, 1, 2, 3) and the number of shortest routes from Ana (1, 1, 1, 2, 2).

figures.caption: Property tests check rules that hold for every network, so they need no hand-worked answer. The notes under each card are checks actually run on the friendship network.
figures.alt: Six cards in two rows. Relabeling changes nothing; distances are symmetric; no shortcuts through a third person; a new tie never hurts; degrees add up to twice the ties; same input gives the same output. Each carries a note on a check made on the ten-person friendship network.

checks: No shortcuts through a third person
Degrees add up to twice the ties

figures.caption: The difference between 0.1 + 0.2 and 0.3 is about 5.6e-17, which is rounding, not error. A tolerance draws the line between that and a real discrepancy such as a score that is off in the second decimal place.
figures.alt: A horizontal line from 1e-17 to 1 on a log scale. A green zone on the left, up to a billionth, is labeled rounding noise: accept. A red zone on the right is labeled too big to be rounding. A green dot sits far left for 0.1 plus 0.2 versus 0.3; a red dot sits at 0.01 for a wrong closeness score.

figures.caption: Fuzzing means testing with many random inputs. Blue bars: how often tiny networks from a typical random generator (distinct pairs only) contain each awkward feature. Orange bars: the same when the generator is told to add self-ties, repeats and a lonely person on purpose.
figures.alt: Six pairs of horizontal bars, one pair per feature: no ties at all, someone with no friends, two or more islands, a person tied to themselves, the same tie listed twice, and all of those at once. The blue bars for the typical generator are empty for self-ties, repeated ties and all of those at once (0 percent each), and the orange bars for deliberate generation are long.

figures.caption: No single check is enough. Together they cover plain mistakes, broken rules, disagreement with other tools, strange inputs and old bugs coming back.
figures.alt: Five horizontal bands stacked like a pyramid, widest at the bottom. From the bottom: hand-checked tiny cases, property tests, reference tools, fuzzing, and regression tests at the top. Each band names what it catches.

figures.caption: Disagreement is not always a bug. These six questions have more than one defensible answer, so a careful comparison fixes the convention first.
figures.alt: A table with six rows and four columns: the question, what one tool says, what another says, and why they can differ. Rows cover self-ties, closeness with unreachable people, clustering for a person with one friend, betweenness raw or scaled, the choice among tied shortest routes, and repeated ties between a pair.
